lead: An intermediate representation (IR) is a form of the program that sits between the source text and the machine code. The front end writes it, the back end reads it, and neither side needs to know the other. Because the IR hides the source language and the target machine at once, one front end can feed several machines and one back end can serve several languages. Postfix is the smallest member of this family: every operator follows its operands, so a stack evaluates it with no brackets and no precedence table. Calculators, JVM bytecode and many compiler back ends use this idea.
prereq: You need: 4.2 Syntax trees and DAGs for expressions for the tree-shaped forms, and Unit 1, Compiler Structure and Lexical Analysis, for the order of the phases.

sections.h3: Why a compiler builds an intermediate form

blocks.text: Source languages are many and machines are many. A translator written directly for one source language and one machine forces a new program for every pair: m source languages and n machines need m × n compilers.

blocks.where: m is the number of source languages and n the number of target machines; writing each front end and each back end once against a shared IR gives m + n halves instead of m × n whole compilers.

blocks.text: An IR is a form of the program that keeps the meaning and drops the surface. The front end — lexer, parser, semantic checks — builds it; the back end — optimiser and code generator — consumes it. Inside a single compiler the IR still pays: an optimisation written once against the IR works for every source language, and the IR is simpler than the source, with no comments, no brackets and no synonyms.

items: Machine independent: no registers and no instruction sizes.
Compact: small enough to stay in memory.
Cheap to walk: easy to build from the parse tree and easy to turn into target code.

blocks.text: Four IRs cover most of this unit. They differ in shape, not in meaning; all four can be built from the same syntax tree using the semantic rules of 4.1.

items: Tree-shaped forms keep nesting visible; the syntax tree and the DAG are covered in 4.2.
Linear forms are read left to right in a single pass.
Postfix keeps operator symbols, so it stays close to the written expression.
Three-address code gives a name to every intermediate value, which is what the optimiser needs; its tables are in 4.5.

blocks.text: The choice trades convenience for use. Trees suit analysis, because a routine can be called on each node. Linear forms suit code generation, because the generator only moves forward. Many real compilers keep two: a tree or graph while checking and optimising, then a linear form for the back end.
Infix puts the operator between its operands: a + b. Prefix, also called Polish notation, puts it before: + a b. Postfix, also called reverse Polish notation, puts it after: a b +.
postfix(E₁ op E₂) = postfix(E₁) postfix(E₂) op
blocks.where: E₁ and E₂ are the operand subexpressions and op is a binary operator; apply the rule from the innermost operator outwards, using the precedence of the grammar.

blocks.text: Because position fixes the order, postfix needs no brackets and no precedence table. (a + b) × c becomes a b + c ×, and a + b × c becomes a b c × +. The brackets of the first version are not lost; they are encoded in where the + sits.

items: Read the tokens from left to right and keep one stack of values.
A binary operator: pop the right operand, then the left, apply the operator and push the result.
At the end exactly one value remains on the stack; it is the answer.

blocks.text: Order matters for − and ÷. In a − b the string is a b −: the first pop gives b, the second gives a, and the result is a − b. Popping in the other order would compute b − a.

A valid postfix string with k operands has exactly k − 1 binary operators. Read the string left to right: after every prefix except the whole string, the number of operands seen is at least one more than the number of operators seen; the difference may be larger than one. Only when the whole string has been read is the difference exactly one, with one value left on the stack. Counting is a quick check in an exam.

spec.aria: Five stack snapshots, one per token of 3 4 2 * +: the stack grows to 3, 4, 2, the * replaces 4 and 2 by 8, and the + replaces 3 and 8 by 11.

examples.question: Using the grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → num, convert 3 + 4 * 2 to postfix. Then evaluate the string with a stack, showing the stack after every token, and state the value of the multiplication and the value of the whole expression.
steps: The grammar makes * bind tighter than +, so 4 * 2 is one subexpression. Its postfix form is 4 2 *.
Replace that subexpression inside the sum: the postfix string is 3 4 2 * +.
Read *: pop 2 as the right operand, pop 4 as the left, 4 × 2 = 8, push 8. Stack is [3, 8].
Read +: pop 8 as the right operand, pop 3 as the left, 3 + 8 = 11, push 11. Stack is [11].
One value remains, so the expression's value is 11.
examples.answer: The postfix form is 3 4 2 * +, the product 4 × 2 is 8, and the whole expression evaluates to 11.

traps: For a − b the postfix string is a b −, never b a −. The first pop is the right operand, the second is the left.
Reversing a postfix string does not give its prefix form. a + b is + a b in prefix and a b + in postfix; reversing a b + gives + b a, which means b + a.
Postfix carries no brackets, so writing (a b +) c × in an answer is wrong.
Postfix is not three-address code: three-address code has names and one operator per instruction, postfix is still one expression.
Examiners give strings with the wrong operator count. A string with k operands must have exactly k − 1 binary operators; check the count before you evaluate.

quiz.q: Define prefix and postfix notation in one line each.
quiz.a: Prefix (Polish): the operator comes before its two operands, as in + a b. Postfix (reverse Polish): the operator comes after them, as in a b +.

quiz.q: Why can postfix be evaluated without a precedence table?
quiz.a: The order of the tokens already fixes the evaluation order. Each operator appears exactly when the values of its two operands are on top of the stack, so no token ever waits for a later, higher-precedence operator.
a b + c d - * . The left bracket group gives a b +, the right group gives c d -, and the outer * joins the two results.

quiz.q: Evaluate the postfix string 6 2 3 * - 4 + with a stack and give the final value.
quiz.a: Push 6, 2, 3 → [6, 2, 3]. * replaces 2 and 3 by 2 × 3 = 6 → [6, 6]. - gives 6 − 6 = 0 → [0]. Push 4 → [0, 4]. + gives 0 + 4 = 4. Final value 4.

quiz.q: A postfix string has 5 operands and 3 binary operators. Is it valid? Why?
quiz.a: No. A valid string with k operands needs exactly k − 1 operators, here 4. With only 3 operators, two values would still be on the stack at the end, so the string is malformed.

quiz.q: Give one reason a compiler may prefer three-address code over postfix for optimisation.
quiz.a: In postfix a repeated subexpression has to be recomputed, because no name refers to its value. Three-address code names each value (t1 = b * c), so a common subexpression is computed once and reused, and dead instructions are easy to spot.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real stack machines — the JVM, the .NET CLR and the WebAssembly virtual machine — compile to a bytecode whose arithmetic is postfix-shaped, because a stack needs no register allocator. Register machines usually take a different IR: LLVM IR and GCC's GIMPLE are three-address-like lists, and modern versions keep them in static single assignment form. Forth and the Hewlett-Packard calculators made reverse Polish famous outside compilers. Search next for 'stack machine bytecode', 'reverse Polish notation calculator' and 'LLVM IR'.
